raw_comment: This graph is a very unique application of simple data collecting. In addition to providing us all with information concerning the travel efficiency, the commuter has also created a hobby which can occupy her time taking said train. Fortunately, many times the train is not excessively late as there are many gray areas in the scarf. In addition, these usually come in larger blocks of color symbolizing a longer span of days where the train was not too late. The pink areas are interspersed less often than the grey, but they occur regularly enough that one can assume that this train runs behind schedule for about a third of the time it runs. The red spaces, representing the longest wait time for trains or delays in both directions occurs much less often except in one outlier. On the right side of this graph, there is one solid chunk of red. This could represent a time when the transit system was dealing with renovations, working on a light schedule, or dealing with inclement weather, such as a season's worth of snow. Either way, there was a major obstacle in the Munich transit system which caused the train to be excessively late during that period. A good headline would be, "Weaving in and out of traffic".

raw_comment: In this graph, I do not see something that looks like a graph at all. In all honesty I see a scarf. It is broken up into three separate colors: red, white, and blue. It could just be the weaver's preference of fabric, but I believe that it could relate to the different sides of the political spectrum. Rarely are the red and blue pictured next to each other, almost always separated by a stripe of white, a barrier of sorts. This could represent how most times, democrats and republicans are unable to work together to form policy in America. It probably represents some form of data, but I am unsure of whether it relates to laws being passed, or percentages of people getting laws passed.

1. Something I notice is that there are delays almost every day. I think this is because a large part of the German rail system was built under the command of Hitler, which means that it is old and dangerous. In an attempt to make these lanes safer, the German government may be trying to repair or modernize the system, which could be the cause of most delays.

2. I also believe that because of all the delays, people have had to change their way of life. Consecutive train delays could have changed people's expectations about the train schedule. This means that people already expect the train to arrive late instead that on time. This could have made them wake up earlier to take the train before the time they do so they can be on time for their jobs or activities.

raw_comment:
My middle school students (ages 11-14) enjoyed thinking about 'What's going on in this past week's graph/scarf?'  

Here are some of their catchy headlines:
- The two rowed scarf (with delays)
- Scarves, Delays, and Graphs, oh my!
- Our Daily Commute, ---- One Person, One Drive, One Scarf --- 40 Minutes To 2 Hours
- Stripes of Time and Memory 
- To Commute if Knot to Remember 
- Threads of Delay and Destiny 
- The Scarf That Delayed the World!
- Woman creates most meaningful scarf in history!
- Scarf Tells Driving Story

We look forward to making this a part of our Instruction Technology curriculum going forward :)

1. What the scarf looks like it represent is the travel times from the beginning of the year which means that the red section would be around early February maybe late January. I wonder as to why the delays were so significant during this period in time and why they were very consistent for what could be assumed as around 5 to 6 days. This extreme patch was then still followed by a series of still very stable but long waiting times. Could this have come from people taking a holiday in Germany and them wanting to explore both the urban and countryside areas of the beautiful landscape?
2. What does this commuter want to reveal with this publication her wait times throughout the course of the year? Could she possibly want to bring the inconvenient wait times of public transport to the officials who are able to control whether or not this is a fixable task? Could she possibly have wanted the people who are possibly thinking about using public transit a little preview of what might come if they also decide to take the public transportation throughout Germany? It could be either or both of these reasons because this woman had to have had some sort of end goal to strive for once she finished her year. She might have thought about how the systems were flawed and needed some rearranging and also could help a few folks from suffering the same wait along the way.

- **Faceted timeline / career timeline chart** with **stacked interval blocks** for each person.

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses **small multiples / faceting by candidate**: four vertical panels, one per candidate.
- Within each panel, career periods are shown as **stacked contiguous rectangles** along a shared vertical time/age scale.
- Uses **color coding** to distinguish career-category types.
- Panels are also grouped under **party headers** (Republican ticket, Democratic ticket).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate vertical panels; name label at top |
| Party ticket | Categorical/nominal | Group header labels spanning panels |
| Age | Quantitative | Position on vertical axis (y-axis) with tick labels |
| Career moment / role | Categorical/nominal | Text labels inside blocks |
| Start year / event year | Temporal | Implied by vertical placement of block start and year labels in text |
| Duration / time span of role | Quantitative/temporal | Height/length of rectangular blocks |
| Career category (College, Military, Private sector, Public service or politics, Federal government, Candidate for federal office) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of blocks |
| Birth year / birthplace | Temporal + categorical/nominal | Subtitle text beneath candidate name |

raw_comment:
(1) The lack of a good public transportation system is an issue that needs to be addressed and dealt with. This woman creatively demonstrates that the countryside of Germany is suffering from efficient public transportation through the color coordination on the scarf. This issue is imperative because countryside folks in Germany need to get to their workplace, house, or destination which requires urgency. Overall, these people on public transportation need a better ride because there is no other way for them to travel and therefore solving this issue can truly only benefit Germany as a whole. 
2) I wonder why this woman would dedicate her time to creating a scarf that only has colors to distinguish the delays of the public transportation she rides on. If she truly intended to show the delays then she should have labeled the scarf with its proper meaning and not just assume that everyone knows what exactly the colors pink, gray, and red represent. Aside from that, she might have simply wanted to get rid of her boredom as she was waiting or even to play a game with the transportation to see if she can predict whether it will be delayed or not.

raw_comment: I have never seen something like this and it is absolutely intriguing to me. This woman was able to use something she is clearly passionate about, knitting, as a way to express information. However, is she simply expressing information, or is she trying to prove a point? Clearly, the woman has taken notice of the delays on her German commute. My assumption is that she is annoyed by it and wants to bring attention to it as she took the time to knit her observations. It appears that most of the delays were either under five minutes or under thirty minutes. However, towards the end of the (what I'm assuming is a) scarf, there is one very long red block, indicating a delay. I wonder if something happened in Germany, perhaps a major current event/story, that caused there to be so much delay on the commute.

## 1) Chart type
- **Faceted timeline / career timeline chart** with **stacked interval blocks** for each person.

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses **small multiples / faceting by candidate**: four vertical panels, one per candidate.
- Within each panel, career periods are shown as **stacked contiguous rectangles** along a shared vertical time/age scale.
- Uses **color coding** to distinguish career-category types.
- Panels are also grouped under **party headers** (Republican ticket, Democratic ticket).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate vertical panels; name label at top |
| Party ticket | Categorical/nominal | Group header labels spanning panels |
| Age | Quantitative | Position on vertical axis (y-axis) with tick labels |
| Career moment / role | Categorical/nominal | Text labels inside blocks |
| Start year / event year | Temporal | Implied by vertical placement of block start and year labels in text |
| Duration / time span of role | Quantitative/temporal | Height/length of rectangular blocks |
| Career category (College, Military, Private sector, Public service or politics, Federal government, Candidate for federal office) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of blocks |
| Birth year / birthplace | Temporal + categorical/nominal | Subtitle text beneath candidate name |

raw_comment: When examining this graph, the frontmost thought in my mind is that this is a very unique graph; I have never seen data represented by a scarf. Concurrently, I find it to be innovative and refreshing. Second to that, I notice that the thickness of the lines is greatest in the first two thirds of the scarf and thinnest towards the last one third. Based on this observation, I can infer that the woman experienced more frequent delays in the first two thirds of her year than she did in the remainder.  The wide red row also catches my eye. Both because red is indicative of a delay that was of more than half an hour or delays in both directions and because of its magnitude, I infer that there must have been an enormous accident that caused hours of delays, or perhaps even that the woman herself got into an accident. Since, as stated earlier, red represents up to 30 minute delays or delays in both directions and yet there lies this massive red row but also very slim red rows, I think the graph would be more logical if the woman incorporated a new color that would represent half an hour or greater. I wonder how this might compare to her commute in future years, as transportation technology continues to advance? Also, how would this graph differ if she decided to bike, walk, or take the train instead of driving to work?

raw_comment: When I first looked at this image, I thought I was on the wrong site. To me, at first glance, this did not look like a graph. I noticed that the gray and pink stripes were more frequent than the red, yet the red took up a very large amount of space 3/4 of the way down the rectangle. I wondered if this served as a type of morse code. I then decided to read the caption, and came to the conclusion that the woman who knitted this "graph" made a very intelligent decision. People notice things out of the ordinary; curiosity kills the cat. After this statement, I would not be surprised if the Munich train station decided to make some changes. I wonder if this blew up online... This woman combined an older skill of knitting with new, fresh, original thought. I wonder how long the gigantic red spot delay was, what caused it, and if there was any compensation. A catchy headline for this graph could be, "In with the old and the new".

I, first and foremost, noticed that this graph was very different from most of the graphs that we see. With this being said, there were still some weird things that I noticed was that there was a large block of red, spanning multiple weeks. Other things that I noticed was that multiple times, there were grey-red-grey patterns. And lastly, there was a lot of color switching near the end.
I wondered why is the large red spot there? Why are there the grey-red-grey patterns? Why is there so much grey near the start? And why are the colors switching so much near the end?

My title is "Knitting Through the Rows of Traffic"

raw_comment: I noticed a few things about this graph. Firstly, there is a period in it where there was a delay of over 30 minutes for around a month in a row. Additionally, there are very many periods of 5 days in a row with grey. These are most likely periods of work days, Monday through Friday, where there are a lot of people commuting to work, increasing the number of time delays. I also noticed that there are periods of multiple days in a row with pink following the gray areas, meaning that there isn't very much traffic on the weekends in this area. I firstly wonder what could have inspired this scarf to be? Why did the creator decide to make this scarf based on their commute to work times? There are a lot of questions that can be asked about why this scarf was created and how inspiration was found to create it. I believe that in this graph a person is commuting to Munich for whatever reason, and that during their trips they are encountering a bit of traffic on the work days because there are also other people that are attempting to get to Munich to work. The period where there was an extended period of 30+ minute delays was most likely a main road closure. There is probably one main road that goes into Munich, and a side road or two. Since the main road was closed down, there was more traffic forced into the side roads, causing greater traffic backup and more time to get through the increase in traffic.

The large patch of red (delays more than 30 minutes or delays in both direction) could be the result of some kind of construction or event that lasted a certain amount of time before returning to normal. Because there are 2 scenarios assigned to the red color, it is hard to tell what exactly caused that large patch of red.

- **Faceted timeline / career timeline chart** with **stacked interval blocks** for each person.

- Uses **color coding** to distinguish career-category types.
- Panels are also grouped under **party headers** (Republican ticket, Democratic ticket).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate vertical panels; name label at top |
| Party ticket | Categorical/nominal | Group header labels spanning panels |
| Age | Quantitative | Position on vertical axis (y-axis) with tick labels |
| Career moment / role | Categorical/nominal | Text labels inside blocks |
| Start year / event year | Temporal | Implied by vertical placement of block start and year labels in text |
| Duration / time span of role | Quantitative/temporal | Height/length of rectangular blocks |
| Career category (College, Military, Private sector, Public service or politics, Federal government, Candidate for federal office) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of blocks |
| Birth year / birthplace | Temporal + categorical/nominal | Subtitle text beneath candidate name |

raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's moderation of  “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  
Today’s graph shows the length of daily delays for 2018 on what should be a 40-minute commute between Munich and a Bavarian town.  The commuter knitted two rows each day.  Grey is for delays under 5 minutes.  Pink is for delays 5 – 30 minutes.  Red is for delays over 30 minutes or delays in both directions.

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, give us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and  "What's going on in this graph?"  
Plus, please have your students share with us a catchy headline that captures your ideas about the graph. 
Tomorrow afternoon, we’ll reveal the New York Times article that included this graph and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.
(The next “What’s Going On in This Graph?” will be released tomorrow, Thursday, Feb. 28 with moderation on Wednesday, March 6.  The topic:  vaping.)

raw_comment: We noticed the big red section and wondered if it had anything to do with the season that she was commuting in - was it in the autumn or winter? We then realized that the kind of transportation was important to the conversation - train or bus (no car - too hard to knit)? We think it might have been a bus because we don't know why trains would be delayed. We also noticed that there seemed to be some sort of delay everyday since there was not a color designated as "no delay". We also noticed that the scarf is narrower in places - indicating tighter stitching - maybe she was stressed or focused during these times. We thought that the looser knitting might indicate that she was more relaxed. We did some math and estimated that there were about 270 rows - representing 135 days of travel. We know that there are more work days in a year so we think she did this just for a season.

## 1) Chart type
- **Faceted timeline / career timeline chart** with **stacked interval blocks** for each person.

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses **small multiples / faceting by candidate**: four vertical panels, one per candidate.
- Within each panel, career periods are shown as **stacked contiguous rectangles** along a shared vertical time/age scale.
- Uses **color coding** to distinguish career-category types.
- Panels are also grouped under **party headers** (Republican ticket, Democratic ticket).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate vertical panels; name label at top |
| Party ticket | Categorical/nominal | Group header labels spanning panels |
| Age | Quantitative | Position on vertical axis (y-axis) with tick labels |
| Career moment / role | Categorical/nominal | Text labels inside blocks |
| Start year / event year | Temporal | Implied by vertical placement of block start and year labels in text |
| Duration / time span of role | Quantitative/temporal | Height/length of rectangular blocks |
| Career category (College, Military, Private sector, Public service or politics, Federal government, Candidate for federal office) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of blocks |
| Birth year / birthplace | Temporal + categorical/nominal | Subtitle text beneath candidate name |
